paragraphs: This paper studies how a social media platform can discourage misinformation sharing by choosing what information to communicate to users. The starting point is that platforms can predict both a post’s likely popularity and its misinformation characteristics, while users are largely motivated to share popular content. This informational advantage creates an opportunity to influence sharing decisions through carefully designed signals.

The authors formulate this interaction using Bayesian persuasion and express the optimal signaling scheme as a linear program, allowing predictions to be imperfect. They also establish necessary and sufficient conditions on the classifier for the platform’s optimal utility to have particular continuity and non-decreasing properties. These results connect the quality of the prediction system to the behavior of the persuasion strategy.

The analysis then includes feedback: platform interventions can change how users behave in the future. The paper characterizes convergence and stability in this performative setting. Experiments report significant misinformation reductions both in a single round and when behavior evolves, supporting the approach within the settings studied.
icml-2024-a-persuasive-approach-to-comba.tldr: Strategically communicating predictions about posts can reduce misinformation sharing, including in experiments where users adapt to platform interventions.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a decision policy from an existing dataset rather than collecting new experience during training. This paper considers linear Markov decision processes with an infinite horizon and discounted rewards: the objective values rewards across an ongoing sequence of decisions while giving less weight to more distant outcomes.

The challenge is to achieve both computational efficiency and favorable data requirements without demanding uniform coverage of the environment by the dataset. The authors introduce a primal-dual algorithm that operates under a partial coverage assumption. They report the first computationally efficient algorithm in this setting with sample complexity proportional to the inverse square of the desired accuracy tolerance.

This improves on a recent method whose sample requirement scales with the inverse fourth power of that tolerance. Thus, the stated improvement concerns how quickly data requirements grow as a more accurate policy is requested. The authors also extend the algorithm to constrained offline learning, where the policy must satisfy requirements on additional reward signals. The guarantees remain tied to the specified linear setting and coverage assumption.
icml-2024-a-primal-dual-algorithm-for-of.tldr: A computationally efficient offline reinforcement learning algorithm achieves inverse-square accuracy sample complexity under partial data coverage and extends to constrained policies.

paragraphs: Training often involves a main objective alongside an auxiliary objective, such as robustness or performance on another dataset. Simply adding the two losses makes them compete through a combined gradient. This paper instead treats the auxiliary objective as something to improve among solutions that minimize the main training loss, giving the two objectives an explicit order of priority.

The resulting method, Bloop, combines the main loss gradient with a component of the auxiliary gradient that is orthogonal to it. This geometric construction is central to how the method balances the objectives. However, when gradients are estimated from mini-batches, preserving the intended orthogonality requires care. The authors explain how an exponential moving average of training gradients helps maintain this property.

Experiments in language processing and computer vision show that Bloop can substantially outperform gradient surgery methods that do not use this moving average. The contribution therefore links an optimization formulation to a practical issue in stochastic training: the direction used to define the auxiliary update matters, as does how that direction is estimated.
icml-2024-careful-with-that-scalpel-impr.tldr: Bloop uses a moving average of training gradients to preserve the orthogonality central to balancing a main loss with an auxiliary objective.

paragraphs: A classifier can influence who chooses to be evaluated by it. If people benefit from receiving a favorable prediction, they may decide whether to participate based on the classifier they expect to face. This paper studies that form of strategic behavior, making participation itself part of the learning problem.

The authors examine learning approaches with increasing awareness of this self-selection. Their analysis follows both directions of the interaction: users’ participation decisions affect learning, and the learned classifier affects the composition of the participating population. This matters because the population a model encounters can depend on the model’s own decision rule, rather than remaining fixed throughout the process.

Building on this analysis, the paper introduces a differentiable framework that incorporates self-selective behavior and can be optimized effectively. Experiments combine real data with simulated user behavior and demonstrate the approach’s utility. The findings support accounting for strategic participation when designing classifiers, with the experimental evidence specifically reflecting the simulated behavioral responses used in the study.
icml-2024-classification-under-strategic.tldr: A differentiable learning framework accounts for users strategically deciding whether to participate in response to a classifier.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model can make inference cheaper, but retaining ordinary task performance does not establish that its trustworthiness has been preserved. This study evaluates three leading language models using five compression techniques across eight trustworthiness dimensions. It examines how efficiency changes interact with properties that benign task evaluations can miss.

Within these experiments, quantization offers a better balance of efficiency and trustworthiness than pruning. A reported 4-bit quantized model preserves its original counterpart’s trustworthiness, whereas pruning significantly harms trustworthiness even at 50% sparsity. The findings also show that moderate quantization can improve particular dimensions, including ethics and fairness, so the relationship is not simply that more compression always causes worse outcomes.

At very low precision, however, the picture changes: 3-bit quantization tends to substantially reduce trustworthiness. These results make the compression choice and its severity relevant to evaluation, beyond whether standard task scores remain strong. The paper’s practical implication is that compressed models need comprehensive trustworthiness assessment because benign performance alone does not reveal the observed risks.
icml-2024-decoding-compressed-trust-scru.tldr: Compression affects LLM trustworthiness in ways ordinary task scores miss, with moderate quantization outperforming pruning in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: A language model can be uncertain because the input leaves multiple interpretations open, or because its training has not supplied enough information. These correspond to different sources of uncertainty, and distinguishing them can help explain an unreliable prediction. This paper introduces input clarification ensembling as a framework for separating these sources in pretrained language models.

The method generates several clarifications of an input, obtains the model’s predictions for each, and combines those predictions. When data uncertainty comes from ambiguity or underspecification in the input, this procedure allows the original prediction to be factored into separate data and model uncertainty terms. The decomposition resembles one used in Bayesian neural networks, while the framework can be applied to any pretrained LLM.

Evaluations on several language processing tasks report accurate and reliable uncertainty quantification. The key qualification concerns the source of data uncertainty: the stated decomposition addresses uncertainty arising from ambiguous or incomplete inputs. The findings support clarification as a useful way to investigate why a model is uncertain, alongside measuring how uncertain it is overall.
icml-2024-decomposing-uncertainty-for-la.tldr: Combining predictions across clarified inputs can separate ambiguity-related uncertainty from model uncertainty in pretrained LLMs.

paragraphs: Online batch selection aims to reduce training costs by choosing informative subsets of data during learning. Some approaches use an additional reference model to judge examples, which becomes difficult when a suitable reference is unavailable. Other approaches avoid that dependency but score examples independently, potentially selecting many samples that contribute similar information.

Diversified Batch Selection, or DivBS, addresses both concerns through a reference-free selection procedure that evaluates samples as a group. Its objective measures orthogonalized representativeness, making redundancy within the selected set part of the decision. The central idea is that a useful batch should represent the data through complementary examples, rather than consist solely of individually attractive samples.

The paper also provides a principled implementation designed to make selection efficient, since choosing a batch must not consume the savings it is intended to create. Experiments across various tasks report a substantially better trade-off between model performance and training speedup. These findings support treating batch composition as a collective selection problem when accelerating training.
icml-2024-diversified-batch-selection-fo.tldr: DivBS accelerates training by selecting diverse, representative batches without a reference model and reports an improved performance–speed trade-off.

paragraphs: Strong code completion and editing performance leaves an underlying question unanswered: how well do code models understand the logical constructs in the programs they process? This paper investigates that question directly. Its focus is the degree of programming concept understanding exhibited by autoregressive models, rather than their success at producing code alone.

The authors introduce Counterfactual Analysis for Programming Concept Predicates, abbreviated CACP. It is a testing framework that uses counterfactual analysis to evaluate programming concepts. The method needs only black-box access to a model, so the evaluation does not depend on inspecting its internal representations or parameters. This makes the proposed test applicable through the model’s observable behavior.

Using CACP, the authors evaluate ten popular large code models on four programming concepts. Their findings suggest that current models lack understanding of concepts including data flow and control flow. The result is evidence about conceptual understanding under this evaluation, and it explains why impressive coding task performance alone does not settle the question of whether a model grasps program logic.
icml-2024-do-large-code-models-understan.tldr: Black-box counterfactual tests of ten code models suggest gaps in understanding programming concepts such as data flow and control flow.

paragraphs: Mixture distributions can make variational inference more expressive, but adding components can also make it expensive. The paper identifies two scaling problems: learnable parameters can increase linearly with the number of components, while evaluating the evidence lower bound can make inference time increase quadratically. These costs restrict how much mixture complexity is practical.

The proposed Multiple Importance Sampling Variational Autoencoder, or MISVAE, shares the mapping from inputs to mixture parameters using one-hot encodings. Under this design, each extra component adds only a negligible number of network parameters. The authors also introduce two estimators for the mixture evidence lower bound, targeting the separate computational cost of evaluating the training objective.

Together, these contributions support hundreds of mixture components and yield better estimation in less time with fewer parameters than previous mixture VAEs. The paper reports state-of-the-art MNIST results and evaluates the estimators in other variational inference settings. In Bayesian phylogenetic inference, the estimators improve inference times for a state-of-the-art mixture model across eight datasets, extending the evidence beyond the VAE architecture.
icml-2024-efficient-mixture-learning-in-.tldr: MISVAE and two new objective estimators make variational inference with hundreds of mixture components more parameter-efficient and faster.

paragraphs: Supervised dimension reduction seeks a smaller description of the inputs that preserves information relevant to predicting an outcome. Sufficient dimension reduction formalizes this aim through conditional independence: the reduced representation should account for the predictive relationship. This paper develops a new theory and method for that task in single-index models.

The method builds on Hellinger correlation, a measure of statistical dependence. The authors use it to identify the dimension reduction subspace and provide theoretical justification for doing so. The choice of dependence measure is central because the reduction must retain the relationship between inputs and the outcome, rather than merely find a compact description of the inputs themselves.

Extensive numerical experiments report significant improvements over existing sufficient dimension reduction methods. The authors attribute these gains largely to better characterization of data dependencies and refinements to existing techniques. The contribution combines a theoretically supported subspace detection method with numerical evidence of improved performance, within the single-index modeling setting studied in the paper.
icml-2024-enhancing-sufficient-dimension.tldr: A Hellinger-correlation method identifies sufficient dimension reduction subspaces in single-index models and outperforms existing methods in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Buying data can affect more than the buyer’s own payoff: one buyer’s purchase may reduce another buyer’s utility. This paper studies data markets with such negative externalities. Sellers post fixed prices, buyers choose any set of sellers to purchase from, and the market is modeled as a simultaneous game.

The authors first assume that buyers already know their valuations. They analyze whether pure Nash equilibria exist and how much welfare those equilibria deliver. Outcomes without intervention are unfavorable, but the paper proves that a platform-imposed transaction cost can produce a pure equilibrium with strong welfare guarantees for a standard class of externality functions.

The study then allows buyers to learn their valuations through repeated market interactions. The intervention remains feasible in that setting, and the authors consider learning algorithms with low regret for both individual and cumulative utility measures. They also examine a richer externality model. The central contribution is a conditional case for transaction costs as a market-design tool, with guarantees tied to the externality structure being analyzed.
icml-2024-equilibrium-of-data-markets-wi.tldr: Platform transaction costs can support stable, high-welfare data markets under specified negative-externality models, including when buyers learn their valuations.

paragraphs: Learning to solve partial differential equations is difficult when spatial shapes and physical states vary widely. Training data alone may not cover the possible configurations, and predictions can become unreliable when a model ignores physical constraints. This paper develops a graph neural architecture that incorporates conservation laws and physical symmetries into the solver.

Graphs provide a foundation for handling different spatial forms. The authors also examine connections between graph neural networks and traditional numerical solvers, using those connections to integrate conservative principles and symmetries into the architecture. This makes physical structure part of the model’s design, reducing its dependence on learning every relevant behavior solely from examples.

Experiments report substantially better generalization when physical laws are included. In particular, the proposed model shows no significant accuracy degradation on unseen spatial domains in the reported tests, while other models degrade. The finding supports the architectural choice: respecting physical structure can help a learned PDE solver transfer across domain shapes, with the evidence established through the experiments presented.
icml-2024-graph-neural-pde-solvers-with-.tldr: A graph neural PDE solver incorporates conservation and physical symmetries, showing stronger generalization to unseen spatial domains in experiments.

paragraphs: Combining predictions from several models can improve accuracy, but keeping and running all of them is costly. Merging their parameters into one model offers a cheaper alternative, yet independently trained networks may not align in ways that make averaging effective. The paper focuses on improving this alignment before models are combined.

Existing alignment approaches often permute neurons to match one network’s features with another’s. Such matching assumes that a useful one-to-one correspondence exists. CCA Merge uses canonical correlation analysis to align linear combinations of features instead. This broader correspondence can capture relationships between models that a simple rearrangement of individual neurons cannot express.

The authors report better performance than earlier merging methods when averaging models trained on either the same data splits or different splits. They also study the harder case of combining more than two models, where CCA Merge performs significantly better than prior methods. The findings support feature alignment beyond neuron permutations as a practical route toward more effective parameter merging.
icml-2024-harmony-in-diversity-merging-n.tldr: CCA Merge aligns linear combinations of neural features and improves model merging over methods restricted to matching individual neurons.

paragraphs: A backdoor attack implants hidden behavior during training so that particular inputs can later trigger incorrect predictions. This paper introduces IBD-PSC, a detector intended to filter malicious images at test time. Its focus is identifying suspicious incoming inputs through how the trained model responds to controlled changes in its parameters.

The method builds on an observed difference called parameter-oriented scaling consistency. When model parameters are amplified, prediction confidence for poisoned samples remains substantially more consistent than confidence for benign samples. The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting this phenomenon and design an adaptive procedure for selecting which batch normalization layers to scale for detection.

Benchmark experiments report that IBD-PSC is effective and efficient, and that it resists the adaptive attacks evaluated in the study. The approach matters because it uses the response to parameter scaling as a detection signal, going beyond the confidence of a single unchanged prediction. The reported resistance supports the detector under the tested attacks without establishing universal protection against every possible adaptation.
icml-2024-ibd-psc-input-level-backdoor-d.tldr: IBD-PSC detects backdoor inputs using their unusually consistent prediction confidence when selected model parameters are scaled up.

paragraphs: A forecast covering many future steps can have a good average error while making poor predictions at particular steps. This paper observes uneven error distributions in forecasting methods, especially recent transformers on popular benchmarks. It argues that optimizing only the average across the prediction window can leave undesirable concentrations of error.

The proposed approach seeks the best average performance subject to a user-defined upper bound on loss at each forecast step. These loss shaping constraints make the distribution of errors part of the optimization problem. The authors use recent duality results to establish a bounded duality gap despite the problem’s non-convexity, then propose a practical primal-dual algorithm to solve it.

Experiments show competitive average forecasting performance while shaping how errors are distributed across the predicted window. The benefit is therefore control over where forecasting loss occurs alongside maintaining overall performance. The theoretical claim is a bounded gap in the optimization formulation, and the empirical claim is successful loss shaping on the evaluated forecasting benchmarks.
icml-2024-loss-shaping-constraints-for-l.tldr: Per-step loss constraints shape errors across a forecasting window while maintaining competitive average performance in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Compressing large neural networks can reduce deployment costs, but some methods add training overhead or sacrifice accuracy. Low-rank factorization offers another route, although repeated decompositions can be expensive and may be suboptimal for nonlinear networks. Maestro builds low-rank structure directly into training through trainable decomposed layers.

Its low-rank ordered decomposition, called LoD, uses sampling to establish an importance ordering within the decomposed network structure. This ordering allows ranks to be selected separately for individual layers. The theoretical analysis connects the procedure to familiar decompositions in specific linear settings: it recovers singular value decomposition for linear mappings on uniformly distributed data and principal component analysis for linear autoencoders.

For deep networks, the authors report that Maestro can produce smaller models while preserving performance. The same trained structure also supports trading accuracy for latency when deploying to more constrained devices, without retraining. This makes the contribution useful for obtaining different model sizes from a training process, with the exact decomposition equivalences established for the stated linear cases.
icml-2024-maestro-uncovering-low-rank-st.tldr: Maestro learns ordered low-rank layers during training, enabling smaller models and deployment accuracy–latency trade-offs without retraining.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from recorded experience becomes harder when the environment is only partially observed and the data are confounded. This paper develops a model-based offline reinforcement learning algorithm for that setting. It permits general function approximation and establishes efficiency under technical conditions that include partial coverage by the offline data.

The first contribution is an identification result for the effects of actions on rewards and future transitions. Building on it, the authors construct a nonparametric two-stage estimator for off-policy evaluation, which assesses policies using the existing dataset. They then optimize conservatively within confidence regions derived from that estimation procedure, connecting policy selection to uncertainty in the evaluation.

Under the stated conditions, the paper gives a finite-sample upper bound on how far the learned policy is from optimal. The bound has polynomial dependence on sample size and horizon length. The result provides a theoretical learning route through identification, evaluation, and conservative optimization, with its guarantee explicitly depending on the assumptions imposed on the problem and available data.
icml-2024-model-based-reinforcement-lear.tldr: A model-based offline RL method learns policies in confounded, partially observed environments with finite-sample guarantees under technical coverage and estimation conditions.

paragraphs: This paper studies persuasion when several informed senders try to influence the actions of one self-interested receiver. Each sender chooses a signaling policy, and those policies interact strategically. The central question is how to find a Nash equilibrium, where no sender benefits from unilaterally changing its policy.

The authors establish serious computational obstacles: finding an equilibrium in general is PPAD-hard, and even calculating one sender’s best response is NP-hard. These results motivate a shift toward finding local equilibria. The proposed method uses a differentiable neural network to approximate utilities that are nonlinear and discontinuous, and combines it with an extra-gradient optimization algorithm.

In the reported experiments, the method finds local equilibria that Pareto-dominate full-revelation equilibria and equilibria obtained using existing neural networks. Such comparisons indicate improved utilities without making another party worse off in the relevant comparison. The contribution pairs general computational hardness results with an empirical approach to finding beneficial local solutions, rather than claiming to efficiently solve every instance of the full equilibrium problem.
icml-2024-multi-sender-persuasion-a-comp.tldr: After proving multi-sender persuasion is computationally hard, the paper uses neural utility approximation and extra-gradient optimization to find improved local equilibria.

paragraphs: This paper addresses inefficiencies associated with outliers in large transformer models through a new associative memory model, OutEffHop. The model is designed to retrieve stored information in an outlier-efficient way. It also provides an interpretation of the Softmax_1 attention mechanism as an approximation to its memory retrieval process.

That connection leads to Hopfield layers that can replace traditional attention mechanisms and offer better performance after quantization. The theoretical analysis shows that OutEffHop retains and improves desirable properties of standard modern Hopfield models, including fixed-point convergence and exponential storage capacity. The proposal therefore combines a memory-based account of attention with a practical architectural change.

Experiments cover transformer and Hopfield architectures including BERT, OPT, ViT, and STanHop-Net, with comparisons against Clipped_Softmax and Gated_Attention. Across four models, the authors report reductions exceeding 22% in average kurtosis and 26% in the maximum infinity norm of outputs, on average. These measures document changes in output outlier behavior, complementing the reported benefits for performance after quantization.
icml-2024-outlier-efficient-hopfield-lay.tldr: OutEffHop derives attention alternatives from associative memory retrieval, reducing output outlier measures and improving post-quantization performance.

paragraphs: Private user data are often distributed across devices that have limited capacity for model training. Training on those devices also requires computation, communication, and deployment effort. PrE-Text addresses these issues by generating differentially private synthetic text that can subsequently be used to train language models.

Across multiple datasets, small models trained on this synthetic text outperform small models trained on-device at the evaluated privacy budgets of epsilon 1.29 and 7.58. The reported results use nine times fewer rounds, six times less client computation per round, and one hundred times less communication per round. These comparisons connect predictive performance to the operational costs of using distributed private data.

The authors also fine-tune large language models on PrE-Text’s synthetic data and report improved performance on private data across the same privacy budgets. This extends the approach beyond models small enough to fit on user devices. Taken together, the results suggest that differentially private synthetic text can be a better training option than on-device learning under the evaluated conditions.
icml-2024-pre-text-training-language-mod.tldr: PrE-Text generates differentially private synthetic text that improves evaluated model performance while sharply reducing client training and communication costs.

paragraphs: Generative models are often pretrained on large datasets and then fine-tuned to align their behavior with human values. This paper examines the assumption that the earlier, potentially unsafe model weights cannot be recovered from the resulting models. It shows that this assumption can fail when several low-rank fine-tuned versions are available.

The proposed method, Spectral DeTuning, uses a few models fine-tuned with LoRA to recover the weights from before fine-tuning. Its target is the original parameters themselves, making the question more specific than whether a model can be prompted into displaying earlier capabilities. The stated access requirement to multiple low-rank fine-tuned models is central to the recovery setting.

The authors demonstrate the vulnerability with large-scale models, including a personalized Stable Diffusion model and an aligned Mistral model. These examples support the claim that recovery of pre-fine-tuning weights is possible in the studied circumstances. The implication is that the existence of an alignment fine-tuning step alone does not establish that earlier weights are unrecoverable from related released models.
icml-2024-recovering-the-pre-fine-tuning.tldr: Spectral DeTuning can recover pre-fine-tuning model weights from a few LoRA-fine-tuned models, challenging an assumption about alignment protection.

paragraphs: Neural networks can rely on concepts that correlate with a task without being desirable evidence for solving it. Concept-removal methods try to eliminate those signals from the network’s internal representation. The difficulty is that removing a spurious concept can also discard useful task information, damaging both performance and interpretations of what the network has learned.

This paper proposes an iterative algorithm that estimates two low-dimensional subspaces together: one associated with the main task and another with the spurious concept. The subspaces are orthogonal, providing a geometric separation between the two kinds of information. Joint estimation is the central design choice, making preservation of task-relevant features part of the removal procedure.

The authors evaluate the method on Waterbirds and CelebA in computer vision and MultiNLI in language processing. They report better identification of main-task and spurious concepts than existing concept-removal methods, along with better selective removal of the latter. The findings support separating desirable and undesirable information together when editing a learned representation.
icml-2024-removing-spurious-concepts-fro.tldr: Jointly estimating task and spurious subspaces improves selective concept removal while better preserving useful information in benchmark evaluations.

paragraphs: Continual learning seeks to acquire sequential tasks while retaining earlier knowledge. Methods that divide a network into old-task and new-task portions can prevent forgetting, but the paper identifies serious underfitting as the task sequence becomes long. Protecting previous learning is therefore only part of the problem; the model also needs capacity to keep adapting.

The proposed Orthogonal Sparse Network, or OSN, introduces a third network portion for knowledge shared between old and new tasks. A task-aware partitioning procedure selects shared parameters, while sharpness-aware orthogonal sparse learning guides how those parameters are trained. The shared portion is intended to consolidate earlier tasks and fit the new task simultaneously.

Qualitative and quantitative analyses report minimal to no interference with past tasks, described as approximately no forgetting, alongside substantially improved plasticity and capacity. The authors also report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is the explicit treatment of shared knowledge within the network partition, with the retention claim remaining approximate rather than an unconditional promise of zero forgetting.
icml-2024-task-aware-orthogonal-sparse-n.tldr: OSN adds a shared-knowledge network portion to improve continual learning capacity while reporting approximately no forgetting.

paragraphs: Disentangled representation learning needs assumptions that narrow the many possible ways a model can encode data. Tripod combines three such inductive biases in an autoencoder: a quantized, grid-like latent space; collective independence among latent variables; and limited influence of one latent on how other latents affect data generation.

These biases target complementary parts of the system: the latent space, encoder, and decoder. However, the authors find that simply combining existing techniques for them does not produce significant benefits. They therefore adapt the techniques to simplify learning, add stabilizing invariances to important regularization terms, and remove incentives for degenerate solutions. The contribution lies in making the three objectives work together effectively.

Tripod achieves state-of-the-art results on four image disentanglement benchmarks and significantly improves on the naive combination. Experiments also show that all three components are needed for its best performance. That finding supports their complementarity in the evaluated model and benchmarks; it does not establish that every successful disentanglement method must use these same three biases.
icml-2024-tripod-three-complementary-ind.tldr: Tripod adapts three complementary inductive biases to work together, achieving state-of-the-art results on four image disentanglement benchmarks.

paragraphs: The Weisfeiler–Leman hierarchy provides a way to reason about what graph neural networks can distinguish and represent. Earlier results connected the 2-WL test to universal approximation of continuous invariant functions on weighted graphs encoding three-dimensional point clouds. This paper extends that connection toward richer inputs and outputs that transform with the geometry.

The authors first show that PPGN can simulate 2-WL uniformly across point clouds with low complexity. They then extend the tests to point clouds containing both positions and velocities. A further theoretical framework establishes equivariant universality: a simple modification of invariant PPGN can uniformly approximate all continuous equivariant functions within the stated framework.

Building on these results, the authors introduce WeLNet and report state-of-the-art results on N-Body dynamics and GEOM-QM9 molecular conformation generation. The paper thus connects expressiveness theory to a working architecture. Its approximation result concerns what the architecture can represent, while the task results provide separate empirical evidence that the construction is effective in the evaluated applications.
icml-2024-weisfeiler-leman-for-euclidean.tldr: Extensions of 2-WL establish equivariant approximation results and motivate WeLNet, which achieves leading results on two geometric learning tasks.
